Running Toward the Clinic: Speed, Biological Risk and Health in the AI Transition

A plain guide to what gets faster, what gets more dangerous, and why the two cannot be added up yet (illustrated edition)

In brief

Faster AI progress could bring new medicines sooner, but it may also make biological misuse easier, and attacks on hospitals already raise in-hospital deaths. I count all of these in one unit, years of healthy life, and find that whether faster progress helps health on balance cannot be settled from what has been measured. In the model, under its stated conditions, some results hold under every open modelling choice. Once misuse capability is reached inside the window, faster progress can add misuse harm while it stays open. Under the level reading, it adds harm if danger at the threshold exceeds the average on the way there. Under the speed reading, it adds harm when danger rises with speed. At a given speed, suppose a countermeasure that needs no identification of the particular organism or substance arrives after misuse capability and before the window ends. If it lowers danger to a fixed level, needing less capability cuts misuse harm only while capability is what holds up deployment. If future years count the same as present ones (no discounting), a benefit that lasts a fixed time and is counted in full gains nothing from arriving earlier. For hospital ransomware, attacks that disable systems and demand payment, I can put only a bracket on the in-hospital death toll in healthy years. Misuse harm is unmeasured, and I adopt no rule for acting while the balance is unknown.

Part 1. Counting biological risk beside health benefits leaves the balance open

Faster progress in AI could bring new medicines to patients sooner. The same progress might make it easier to cause harm with biology, by an amount no source read measures. Meanwhile, cyberattacks keep hitting hospitals’ computer systems, and some care never reaches the patients it was meant for. The question here is what happens to a population’s health when all of these run off the same clock.

In Running Through the Rain: Speed, Secrecy and Risk in the AI Cyber Transition, I asked whether faster progress in general AI capability should be welcomed when the same capability arms cyber attackers and also brings health benefits. There, the benefits gave a second reason to run, but only on two conditions:

  • the benefit is still waiting on capability, not on clinical trials and regulatory approval; and
  • the health gained from earlier arrival exceeds the added cyber harm.

That ranking set one kind of harm against the benefit. Here I count three: deliberate biological misuse, accidents or insider releases at research facilities, and cyberattacks on the health systems that deliver care. Everything is counted in years of healthy life.

Here is an analogy, and only an analogy. Picture someone deciding whether to run through rain to a far curb. Running shortens the time spent getting wet. Here part of the wait in the rain cannot be shortened by running, because a medicine still has to pass trials and approval. Running may also thicken the rain or reach the heavy downpour sooner, if faster progress raises misuse danger or reaches the misuse threshold earlier.

Four questions follow:

  1. Does the earlier ranking survive?
  2. Where it does not, which mechanism reverses it?
  3. Does the answer depend on how the danger of misuse is written down?
  4. What would have to be observed to settle the rest?

The short answer is that, within the model’s stated conditions, whether faster progress helps health on balance is undetermined. Some results survive every open modelling choice. Others depend on a choice, and the rest turn on quantities for which my search found no measure.

Part 2. The laboratory behind the question is known mainly from its owner’s account

The general question is how an AI developer’s own biology laboratory changes the balance between new therapies and biological risk. The occasion is specific. Reuters reported Anthropic’s biology laboratory on 18 September 2026, and the company described it five days later. Cyber events reported as involving the company are one reason attacks on health systems are counted beside the laboratory.

The public debate my search found is thin and mostly non-expert. It is about legitimacy rather than safety: secrecy, limited outside oversight, and a company that warns of catastrophe now expanding into biology. No study comparing safety was found, and I take no side in that debate.

What is known, and from whom

Two news outlets report that the laboratory exists, and the company confirms it. Its size, staff and opening date are not stated. What it does is known only from the company’s own account, which says:

  • it works on fundamental biology rather than on drug discovery specifically, and does no clinical work for now;
  • it operates only at biosafety levels 1 and 2, two of the lower levels of laboratory containment, and handles no pathogen that can infect humans;
  • human scientists do all the hands-on laboratory work, and having the AI model control laboratory equipment is an aim, not current practice.

By its own description, the company’s wider life-sciences unit includes drug discovery, but nothing I read shows where that work takes place. Going by the company’s statements alone, the laboratory falls outside the high- and maximum-containment facilities that the biosafety sources I read study.

No independent inspection, permit, registration or biosafety committee record was found. The two US oversight regimes considered here are triggered by holding a listed biological agent or receiving federal life-sciences funding. The company’s statements bear only on the first, and nothing read settles the second, so whether the company running the laboratory falls under those rules is undetermined. No measure was found of how the laboratory has affected when any therapy reaches patients. That absence does not show the laboratory is irrelevant to therapies.

Four conditions, reported one at a time

Research on AI-directed laboratories names one way such a facility could lower the barrier of hands-on skill that misuse would otherwise need. It also notes that this has not been tested. Whether technical capability or hands-on skill is what holds misuse back was already contested before AI. On my summary of that research, carrying the concern over to a particular facility takes four conditions. I report each against the company’s account and do not combine them:

  1. Biological rather than chemical work: met.
  2. Automation that replaces skilled hands rather than supervising them: not met as the company reports it, since humans do the bench work and model direction is only an aim.
  3. Carrying out experiments specified by outsiders: unknown, since nothing read addresses it.
  4. Work with agents close to those this research is concerned with: not met as the company reports it.

If humans do the bench work as reported, the route this research names does not apply to that work. That would not rule out AI assistance, or every effect on hands-on skill. The checklist also leaves out one route: laboratory results feeding into model training or testing. That route would enter Part 8’s comparison only if it changed how much capability a countermeasure or misuse needs (their capability distances).

I do not ask whether this laboratory is safe, or safer than a public one, because no source found can answer that. The question is narrower. Suppose a developer-owned laboratory changes how much capability a countermeasure needs and how much capability misuse needs. At a fixed speed of progress, does that pair of changes lower misuse harm? Part 8 gives the model’s answer. Nothing here says which distance the reported laboratory moves, by how much, or how often accidents or releases might happen there.

Part 3. Seven bodies of research each stop short of the question

The search covered seven literatures. Each establishes something, and each stops somewhere.

Growth, catastrophe and speed. This is the research Running Through the Rain builds on. It puts lives saved and catastrophic risk in one unit, which is what makes a ledger of healthy years possible. But it treats catastrophe as a generic one-time event, not as a danger tied to the capability that produces the gain. Its finding that catastrophe costs multiply while health benefits merely add up holds only under specific assumptions about consumption and attitudes to risk. Its strongest objection to haste says new capability is best adopted gradually when damage grows with capability and society learns along the way. That objection rests on learning, which the model in that paper does not include.

AI and biological misuse. The empirical work stops at how well people perform tasks with and without models (Part 11). No source read estimates harm per unit of capability. No real-world misuse harm is recorded, though one developer reports disrupting attempts. Interests run in both directions, and I disclose them rather than adjust my evidence grades (STRONG, MODERATE or WEAK) to account for them:

  • five of the eight controlled trials are developers testing their own models;
  • the physical-laboratory trial was partly funded by the Frontier Model Forum and Sentinel Bio;
  • the authors of the virology benchmark, a test of knowledge about viruses, work at biosecurity organisations (SecureBio and the Center for AI Safety);
  • the review that finds no recorded harm is led from Cohere For AI, with a co-author at Mistral AI alongside academics, and it criticises how immature and opaque the studies are;
  • the report of disrupted plots is a company’s account of its own product.

None of these affiliations invalidates a study’s design. All of them are a reason not to treat agreement within one camp as independent confirmation.

Laboratory safety and research with both beneficial and harmful uses. The legal sources say precisely when oversight applies. US rules reach a laboratory through a listed agent or federal research funding. Canada licenses the activity whoever pays for it, and the treaty read sets duties for each country without checks on individual facilities. The biosafety record read gives no accident rate: two published calculations on one dataset estimate different quantities, and no rate broken down by type of operator was found.

Cyberattacks on health systems. One study that can show cause and effect finds that hospital ransomware attacks reduce the number of inpatients and raise in-hospital deaths among patients already admitted. Studies of single incidents detect no difference in death rates. No source read converts these outcomes into healthy years. What is measured is harm to existing care. Only one abstract, on disrupted clinical trials, bears on delays to a new therapy.

Offence, defence and countermeasures. Formal theory makes the balance between attack and defence depend on how much each side invests, not on a fixed property of the field, and it does not model biology. The one study that asks the biological question directly finds attackers favoured on four of five asymmetries. It does no quantitative analysis and, by choice, limits defence to pharmaceuticals. In the sources read, countermeasure milestones are dated for one vaccine programme. One mathematical model gives a condition under which isolation alone controls an outbreak, but that is not a general limit on how well defence can do.

Trust and ownership. Economics frames the question of who should own a facility around quality that contracts cannot specify and how easily the operator can be replaced, not around who is inherently trustworthy. Public ownership does not remove insider risk. The two pathogen releases these sources attribute to anyone both trace to public military facilities. One is the 2001 mailings, attributed to an insider in a prosecutors’ summary that was never tested at trial. A National Academies review concluded that the scientific evidence alone could not settle their origin. The other attribution was read only in abstract. Public-opinion surveys measure perceived legitimacy, not safety, and no study comparing safety outcomes at private and public life-science facilities was found.

The benefit premise. Part 13 reviews discovery speed-ups, waits for trials and uptake, success rates, narrow clinical tools, and the lack of any estimate of health gained across a population.

None of the sources read models health benefits and biological misuse together in health units. None settles how the danger of misuse is set, either.

Part 4. One yardstick: every healthy year gained or lost, counted once

What is a year of healthy life?

The technical paper’s unit is the disability-adjusted life year, or DALY. One DALY is one year of healthy life lost. Using one unit for benefits and harms is what lets them be set against each other in a single ledger.

The earlier model supplies a speed threshold and a health balance

I take two tools from Running Through the Rain. The first is a count of cyber losses with a speed threshold. It assumes that the attack rate starts above zero and rises with speed, that adoption takes a fixed amount of time and can run alongside capability building, and that a separate contribution to expected losses stays fixed as speed changes. In that model, speeding up lowers cyber loss only while the length of the exposed period is set by how much capability must still be built. At the speed being examined, it also requires the attack rate to be rising less than proportionally with speed. Assuming the attack rate rises with speed, once a fixed adoption time sets the length of the period instead, speeding up only raises loss.

The second tool is a health balance. A therapy delivers a steady flow of healthy years from the day it arrives to the end of a counted window, and that flow is set against cyber losses. Each wait in that model has two parts. One is set by capability, which speed shortens. The other is set by adoption (trials, approval, uptake), which speed does not shorten. For both the cyber and therapy clocks, any part of adoption that runs in parallel can finish during capability building. The clock still has to allow for whichever takes longer, then add any adoption work that can start only once the capability is ready. That model also offers a second way of describing the danger, which Part 5 takes up.

What the ledger adds up

The ledger compares an intervention with a baseline over a window of years. Its entries are:

  • Therapy benefit: a yearly flow of healthy years if the therapy works, times the probability that a candidate found with AI reaches patients. It is counted from arrival to the end of the window, with a reduction for any benefit lost because a developer-owned laboratory withholds findings from outside researchers.
  • Delivery losses: benefit lost when hospital outages interrupt patients on the new therapy, and trial delays caused by cyberattacks, which push the therapy’s arrival later.
  • Baseline care lost in hospital attacks.
  • Biological harms: deliberate misuse, releases from facilities, and harm to facility workers.
  • Two further entries: gains from countermeasures against natural outbreaks, and harm from clean-up after attacks.

Cyber harm outside the health system is left out of the ledger. Two assumptions matter later. First, the success probability is fixed at the point where the benefit becomes possible, so it does not change with speed. Second, misuse and facility releases share one severity class, with a fixed loss per event.

Each life is counted once

The accounting rule is that double counting concerns lives, not causes. Take a hospital attack. The total harm to patients during the outage is split once, into baseline care lost and the extra benefit forgone from the new therapy. Each lost year of healthy life goes into one of the two, never both. In the same way, each biological event goes into one pathway only: misuse, facility release, or harm to facility workers. Simply adding up the entries is an approximation. It holds for small changes in expected losses that do not overlap.

Figure 1 lays out the rule. It is an accounting rule, true because of how the ledger is built, not a finding about the world.

Six interventions, each moving named pieces

The model compares six interventions. Each one moves named quantities and, by assumption, holds everything else fixed:

  • I1, the speed of progress;
  • I2, release, which moves the misuse danger;
  • I3, a developer-owned laboratory, which moves facility releases and worker harm, moves withholding, and may move the success probability and the capability distances for a therapy, a countermeasure and misuse;
  • I4, a public or academic equivalent, which moves facility releases and worker harm and is assumed to withhold nothing;
  • I5, a countermeasure programme, which moves how long deployment takes, the share of adoption that runs after capability arrives, and how much capability the countermeasure needs;
  • I6, oversight, and screening at the point where digital designs become physical material, which moves facility event rates or the misuse danger.

The comparison of I3 with I4 is lopsided. Withholding costs I3 some benefit, but I4’s openness carries no cost for spreading dual-use knowledge. With openness costed on one side only, the ledger supports no comparison of I3 with I4.

Four clocks run at one speed

One speed of progress moves four capability distances: the one cyber attackers need, the one a therapy needs, the one misuse needs, and the one a countermeasure needs (Figure 2). Misuse capability arrives once progress has covered its distance. A countermeasure arrives after two waits: a capability part, which speed shortens, and an adoption part, which it does not. When the capability part is what holds the countermeasure back, in the technical paper it is on its capability branch. When adoption holds it back, it is on its adoption branch.

When the countermeasure lands, the danger of misuse steps to a constant leftover level. Complete closure means the leftover is zero. That step to a constant leftover is an assumption of the model. Because the countermeasure’s clock starts at the beginning, the model covers only countermeasures that do not have to wait for a particular agent to be identified.

How bad each event is stays fixed

In the model, how often misuse events happen can depend on the level of capability or on how fast capability advances. The loss per event stays fixed (Figure 3). Because the ledger adds up expected healthy years, an event that is occasionally enormous still enters through its average loss. That holds as long as the average is finite and each event’s size is unrelated to how many events occur. What holding the loss fixed leaves out is severity that rises with capability, which is the channel the catastrophe literature emphasises.

The counting window leans toward harms

How long the window runs is a modelling choice. Each death inside it is booked, undiscounted, on the date it happens, with all the life-years it costs, including years that fall after the window ends. That keeps the loss per event constant. An ongoing undiscounted benefit flow, by contrast, has a finite value only if it is cut off at the end of the window.

So life-years lost after the window count in full, while life-years gained after it count for nothing (Figure 4). Every undiscounted comparison that sets such death losses, from misuse, hospitals or facilities, against a benefit cut off at the window is tilted toward the harms.

Part 5. Three modelling choices that no source settles

Three times, the biological problem forces a modelling decision that no source in my search settles. Each time I carry both options side by side, as equals. That is a stance about how to model, not a reading of what the field has found.

Is danger set by how far capability has got, or by how fast it is moving?

Another analogy, and only an analogy: a mountain road at night. On one view, the danger is the altitude. The higher you climb, the narrower the road, whatever your speed. On the other view, the danger is the driving: what threatens you is how fast you take the bends.

The first choice is the same fork, applied to misuse. On the level reading (the technical paper’s level-set specification), danger depends on the capability level reached. As capability climbs to the misuse threshold, danger follows the level reached and then holds at a plateau once the threshold is reached. On the speed reading (speed-set), danger depends on the speed of advance and stays constant over the exposed period at any given speed. Running Through the Rain uses the speed form for its main results. Under the speed reading, the model assumes that faster progress means higher danger.

Figure 5 draws both readings.

When does misuse danger start to count?

The second choice is about exposure (Figure 6). On one reading, danger counts from the start (ramp-on), from the first day. On the other, it counts from arrival (arrival-on), only once misuse capability is reached. Under the speed reading, counting from the start means full-strength danger before the misuse capability even exists. Nothing read settles whether that is biologically plausible.

When comparing the level and speed readings with danger counted from arrival, I use a “gated” form of the level reading. That means zero danger below the threshold and full danger at it. Part 8 asks what happens when a facility moves the threshold itself at a fixed speed. Under convention B, the threshold can move along the same smooth danger curve. When danger is counted from arrival, the height of the plateau then depends on where the new threshold lies.

What does “bringing misuse capability closer” mean?

The third choice arises only under the level reading, when a facility running at a fixed speed lets misuse begin at a lower capability level. What then happens to the danger curve has to be assumed, and I use two conventions (Figure 7):

  • Convention A squeezes the whole curve, so danger climbs faster to the same plateau. Counted from the start, misuse loss rises when the plateau danger is higher than the average danger along the climb.
  • Convention B keeps the curve’s shape but stops it at the lower threshold. If danger is rising there, the plateau stops lower. The threshold now does two jobs: it marks when misuse starts and caps how bad it gets. Counted from the start, if danger never falls as capability rises, bringing misuse closer lowers loss or leaves it unchanged. Counted from arrival, its effect under B could go either way.

Counted from the start, the two conventions give strictly opposite effects when plateau danger exceeds the climb’s average and danger is still rising at the threshold. That follows from how the conventions are defined. Treating B as one meaning of “bringing misuse closer” is my modelling choice, and no source found says which describes a real facility.

Figure 8 summarises which results each choice touches. Parts 6 to 10 go through them.

Part 6. Without a defence, faster progress can add misuse harm

Faster progress lengthens the time at full danger

Under the level reading, danger follows capability up to the misuse threshold, then stays at a plateau. Suppose the threshold is reached inside the window and no defence ever lowers the danger. In the technical paper this is the plateau result, R2. Faster progress shortens the climb and lengthens the plateau by exactly the same amount of time (Figure 9). In effect, it swaps time spent at the climb’s average danger for time spent at the plateau’s full danger.

In the model, that swap adds misuse loss whenever the danger at the threshold is higher than its average along the climb. If danger never falls as capability rises, the effect is never negative. It is strictly positive if, in addition, danger has no jumps and is not flat, or in any case whenever the plateau exceeds the climb’s average. With discounting, the effect is still never negative as long as danger never falls.

The speed reading points the same way. Counted from the start, faster progress raises misuse loss whenever danger rises with speed, as the model assumes. The effect is zero at a speed where danger has no immediate response to a small change in speed. Counted from arrival, earlier arrival also lengthens exposure, so the effect is positive whenever danger does not fall with speed, and it stays positive under discounting. Both plateau results apply the algebra of Running Through the Rain to misuse.

With a therapy in the ledger, the test is benefit against misuse

Now set the therapy beside misuse, under these conditions:

  • the therapy waits on capability and arrives inside the window;
  • misuse capability arrives inside the window, and nothing closes it;
  • nothing is withheld, trial delays do not change with speed, and every other effect is set aside.

In the model, speeding up then improves the balance if and only if the healthy years gained from the therapy’s earlier arrival exceed the added misuse loss, also counted in healthy years. When danger is counted from arrival, this holds under the speed reading and under the gated level reading.

Under the level reading counted from the start, the test does not depend on speed, on the window’s length, or on how strongly danger responds to speed. On one side it puts the therapy’s expected yearly benefit times the capability distance the therapy needs. On the other it puts the loss per misuse event, times the misuse distance, times how far the plateau’s danger exceeds the climb’s average. Under the speed reading counted from the start, by contrast, the misuse side grows with the window’s length and with danger’s response to speed. So lengthening the window can turn the speed reading’s verdict against acceleration.

Faster progress can pull a distant danger into the window

Now suppose the misuse threshold lies beyond what progress reaches at the current speed before the window closes (the truncation result, R1). Under the level reading, faster progress reaches higher capability levels before the window closes. So danger that used to lie beyond the window is pulled into the count (Figure 10). If danger never falls as capability rises, this never lowers loss. When danger has no jump at the threshold, the effect of a small change in speed joins the plateau result smoothly as misuse capability starts to arrive inside the window.

Under the speed reading this mechanism does not exist, because danger is not tied to a level. Counted from arrival, misuse loss stays at zero as long as the threshold lies beyond the window. As misuse capability first reaches the end of the window, the plateau calculation begins to count the effect of speed on bringing exposure forward. Counted from the start, faster progress raises loss through higher intensity alone, and the misuse distance plays no part. So truncation is a result of the level reading counted from the start, and it needs a window that ends. In the gated form counted from arrival, level-reading misuse loss is zero while the threshold lies beyond the window. And if the window never ended, any positive speed would reach the threshold eventually.

Beyond the borrowed algebra, four things are new here. They are truncation under the level reading counted from the start, the moving defence date in Part 7, the disagreement between the two readings in Part 10, and the linking of misuse with the benefit and hospital channels.

Part 7. When a defence is on its way, whether speed helps turns on a race

Now suppose a countermeasure steps the danger of misuse to a leftover level on the day it is deployed. In the technical paper, the timing of this is the defence clock, R3. Three conditions apply: misuse capability arrives no later than the countermeasure, the countermeasure lands inside the window, and the leftover level is fixed. The timing order must hold for nearby speeds as well. If the two dates coincide only at one speed and their order changes there, the result covers the effect from the side where misuse arrives first. Because the defence clock starts at the beginning, the result covers only countermeasures that do not have to wait for a particular agent to be identified. For a countermeasure aimed at one particular pathogen, the result is open.

Under the level reading, two distances race

Speeding up now does two things. It brings the countermeasure forward, which ends exposure to the pre-defence danger sooner. Some danger may remain after deployment. It also brings misuse capability forward, which swaps climb for plateau, as in Part 6.

Suppose the countermeasure needs its own amount of capability, its defence distance, and is still waiting on capability. In the model, faster progress then lowers misuse loss if and only if one product beats another:

  • the countermeasure’s side: the defence distance, times the danger the countermeasure removes (plateau danger minus leftover);
  • the misuse side: the misuse distance, times how far plateau danger exceeds the climb’s average.

It is a weighted race between two capability distances (Figure 11). If the countermeasure is instead paced by the misuse distance itself, speeding up lowers loss on the capability branch when the leftover danger is below the climb’s average.

Under the speed reading, two ratios race

Counted from the start, the speed reading turns the race into a comparison of two ratios (Figure 12). The first is how strongly danger responds to speed: the proportional change in danger compared with a very small proportional change in speed. In the technical paper this is the elasticity. The second is the share of the countermeasure’s wait that capability sets, multiplied by the share of the danger the countermeasure removes. In the model, speeding up lowers misuse loss if and only if the first ratio is smaller than the second.

When the countermeasure has its own defence distance, the misuse distance drops out of this test altogether (when defence is paced by the misuse distance, that distance enters the capability share of the wait). With complete closure, no adoption delay left once capability is in hand, and the countermeasure waiting on capability, the test reduces to the one in Running Through the Rain: danger must rise less than proportionally with speed.

Counted from arrival, the misuse distance comes back in, because earlier arrival starts the exposure sooner. Suppose the countermeasure is still waiting on its own capability and lands after misuse arrives. To find the threshold, take the wait for defence capability and multiply it by the share of danger the countermeasure removes. Subtract the wait for misuse capability, then divide the result by the exposed time between misuse arrival and deployment. Speeding up lowers loss if and only if danger’s response to speed is below that threshold. With complete closure, speeding up can lower misuse loss only if the defence distance exceeds the misuse distance. If the defence and misuse arrival dates cross, the effect of speed changes abruptly at the crossing unless no adoption work remains after defence capability is ready or the countermeasure leaves the danger unchanged there. When the countermeasure is paced by the misuse distance and is waiting on capability, speeding up never lowers misuse loss.

Where the countermeasure waits on adoption, both readings agree that speed hurts

Once the countermeasure is waiting on adoption, speed cannot bring it any sooner. In the model, faster progress then raises misuse loss under both readings. Under the level reading this holds when the plateau exceeds the climb’s average. Under the speed reading it holds whenever danger rises with speed, however exposure is counted. If the leftover danger itself responds to speed, each test gains an extra term.

What if danger has both a level part and a speed part? Counted from the start, with complete closure, a threshold of the same kind still exists: danger’s response to speed set against a share of the wait. On the plateau with no defence, though, no such threshold exists. There, if the misuse distance is positive and the level part never falls, no positive response to speed lets acceleration lower loss.

Part 8. At a fixed speed, a laboratory’s effect depends on which distance it moves

Now hold speed fixed. Ask how a laboratory that changes the defence distance and the misuse distance moves misuse loss. The conditions are:

  • misuse capability arrives before the countermeasure, which lands inside the window;
  • the countermeasure’s date does not depend on the misuse distance, and the leftover level is fixed;
  • there is one severity class with a fixed loss per event;
  • the changes stay away from the switch points where a different wait becomes the binding one.

The speed result and the facility result do not settle each other

The race in Part 7 compares the sizes of the two distances. The facility question holds speed fixed and compares changes in them. Under the speed reading, the facility’s effect does not involve danger’s response to speed, while the speed result depends on it. So varying that response can flip the speed result while the facility result stays put. This holds counted either way. Under the level reading with convention A, counted from the start, a worked counterexample in the technical paper’s appendix shows the independence runs in both directions. It is not shown there for convention B or for the level reading counted from arrival.

One exact link remains. At the margin under convention A, with the leftover and the adoption delay held fixed, speeding up by a small percentage has the same first-order effect as cutting both distances by that percentage. Under the speed reading the same link holds with one added term. It counts how much the speed increase changes the intensity of danger over the exposed period before deployment. Under convention B it fails in general.

Shortening the defence distance has the same form of effect under every choice

In the model, shortening the defence distance lowers misuse loss if and only if two things hold: the countermeasure is waiting on capability, and plateau danger exceeds the leftover. This holds under both readings, both ways of counting, and both conventions. Adoption can split into a parallel part that runs alongside capability building and a sequential part that waits until capability arrives; once the capability wait falls below that parallel part of adoption, the countermeasure is on its adoption branch, and further cuts buy nothing (Figures 13 and 14). The result still holds when coverage builds up gradually, as long as the build-up shifts rigidly with the deployment date and finishes before the window ends. It changes if coverage is still rising when the window ends.

What stays the same across the choices is the form of the effect and the condition for its sign, not its size. The reason is that the defence distance moves only one thing, the date the countermeasure lands.

Shortening the misuse distance depends on every choice

The effect of the misuse distance changes with each choice (Figure 15(a)):

  • Level reading, counted from the start. Under convention A, shortening the misuse distance raises loss when the plateau exceeds the climb’s average. For that pair of cuts to lower loss, the cut to the defence distance, weighted by how much danger the defence removes, must outweigh the cut to the misuse distance, weighted by how far plateau danger exceeds the climb’s average. The defence cut helps only while deployment waits on capability. Under convention B, if danger never falls, shortening it lowers loss or leaves it unchanged. So the sign flips between A and B whenever the plateau exceeds the climb’s average and danger is still rising at the threshold.
  • Level reading, counted from arrival. Under A, shortening the misuse distance raises loss. For a pair of cuts, weight the misuse cut by the full plateau danger and the defence cut by the danger the countermeasure removes. The defence cut contributes only while deployment waits on capability, and the pair lowers loss if the weighted defence cut is larger. Under B, the sign is not fixed. For a small cut, with positive danger at the threshold, shortening lowers loss if and only if the proportional response of danger to capability at the threshold exceeds the ratio of the time before misuse arrives to the time from misuse arrival to deployment.
  • If the countermeasure lands before misuse arrives (counted from the start), the effect is zero under B, and under A shortening the misuse distance never lowers loss when danger never falls as capability rises.
  • Speed reading. Counted from the start, the misuse distance has no effect. Counted from arrival, shortening it raises loss. The facility lowers misuse loss if the defence cut, weighted by the danger the countermeasure removes, outweighs the misuse cut, weighted by the full pre-defence danger. The defence cut contributes only while deployment waits on capability. The plain rule “cut the defence distance by more than the misuse distance” applies only with complete closure and a countermeasure waiting on capability.

Within a single regime, under convention A and under the speed reading, these rules hold exactly for changes of any size. Under convention B, larger changes have to be worked out in full rather than read off the rule. Crossing into a different regime can also reverse a prediction, as Figure 15(b) shows.

Part 9. On the benefit side, discounting shifts weight toward earlier arrival

Discounting counts a healthy year that comes sooner as worth more than one that comes later. There are two ways to add benefit: make a candidate therapy arrive sooner (the timing margin), or raise its chance of reaching patients (the probability margin).

Result B: the discount rate tilts timing against probability

Take a therapy with a positive expected benefit that is still waiting on capability. Suppose its benefit continues indefinitely or flows until a finite window closes, and that it arrives before the window closes when there is one. Both margins shrink as the discount rate rises, but the probability margin shrinks faster, in proportion. Compare the extra benefit from a very small percentage increase in speed with the extra benefit from the same percentage increase in the chance of success. In the model, the first gain divided by the second rises steadily with the discount rate (Result B, Figure 16(a)). Which margin is larger depends on that ratio, which turns on unmeasured quantities. If the therapy waits on adoption instead, the timing margin is zero.

The two margins work together: a higher chance of success makes earlier arrival worth more. The success probability is fixed at the point where the benefit becomes possible. If it rose with capability beyond that point, speed would gain a second channel to health.

A benefit of fixed length gains nothing from arriving early unless it is discounted

Now take a benefit that lasts a fixed number of years after it arrives and is counted in full, ending before the window does. Undiscounted, earlier arrival is worth exactly zero. It only slides the same block of healthy years earlier in time. With discounting, when the therapy waits on capability (with a positive expected benefit), the timing margin first rises with the discount rate, at low rates, and then falls at higher rates (as long as arrival is after the start). This is the technical paper’s Corollary (Figure 16(b)). If the therapy is still waiting on capability and arrives before the window ends, earlier arrival raises the undiscounted count for a benefit cut off at the window. More of the benefit fits inside.

No decision rule is offered

One observation is my judgment, not a derived result. For a fixed-length benefit counted in full, the timing argument for hurrying on health grounds relies on discounting the future. It sits beside a case for weighing long-run catastrophe heavily. I do not weigh the two against each other. Nor do I offer a rule for acting while the balance is unknown.

The rule called maximin chooses the option whose worst outcome is least bad. Rawls (1971) defends it only under three special conditions: knowledge of the likelihoods is very insecure, the chooser cares little for gains above the minimum, and the rejected outcomes are unacceptable. Gardiner (2006) adopts these as sufficient conditions for a core precautionary principle.

In this setting, a sign that flips between readings shows that no option is better under every reading. That alone is not a reason maximin cannot apply, and I do not work maximin out. Although the success probability at least lies between zero and one (even though it is unmeasured), two further limits remain:

  • nothing read puts bounds on the benefit flow or on the loss per misuse event;
  • holding the loss per event fixed leaves out severity that rises with capability.

Part 10. Where the two readings of danger disagree, and when that changes the verdict on speed

Both readings fit the documented evidence. I ask where they give strictly opposite answers on whether speed raises misuse loss, sorting the cases into seven rows:

  1. the plateau, with no defence;
  2. truncation, with no defence;
  3. a countermeasure that closes all risk at the moment misuse arrives;
  4. a countermeasure paced by the misuse distance;
  5. a countermeasure that waits on its own defence distance;
  6. a countermeasure waiting on adoption;
  7. the plateau, with the therapy benefit in the ledger.

Rows 3 to 5 assume the countermeasure is waiting on capability, with a fixed leftover. Throughout, danger is assumed to rise with speed under the speed reading.

Counted from arrival, only one disagreement remains

Counted from arrival, and compared like with like using the gated level reading, only row 5 can give opposite answers (Figure 17). Rows 1 and 4 would need negative danger. Row 2 is zero on both sides, row 3 has no version counted from arrival, and in row 6 both readings agree that speed hurts. Row 5 survives because the level reading compares two distances, while the speed reading compares danger’s response to speed with a share of the wait.

Suppose the two readings’ danger is set equal at the speed in question, as a convention for comparing them. Then wherever row 5 diverges, it is the level reading that favours speed. The same direction holds if the defence leaves zero danger, even when the two readings start with different hazard levels. With some danger left after deployment, letting the two scales differ can reverse that.

For row 7, keep that equal-danger convention and count exposure from arrival. Suppose the therapy still waits on capability, both arrivals fall inside the window, and a misuse event carries a positive loss. The speed reading sets a higher bar for the therapy benefit because faster progress also raises the intensity of danger over the exposed period. A benefit that falls between them passes the level-reading test and fails the speed-reading test, and never the other way round.

Counted from the start, more disagreements appear, on a shakier premise

Counting from the start is the secondary case, because its speed-reading premise is unsettled for biology. On that reading, rows 1 to 5 can all give opposite signs. Rows 1 and 2 do so only if danger falls somewhere as capability rises, so for danger that never falls, only rows 3 to 5 can disagree. In row 3, with positive average danger along the climb, the level reading always lowers loss, while the speed reading raises it if and only if danger rises more than proportionally with speed. In row 4, the two can disagree in either direction: the level reading lowers loss if and only if the leftover danger is below the climb’s average, while the speed reading lowers it if and only if danger’s response to speed is below the capability share of the wait times the share of danger removed. In row 5, reversals happen between two thresholds and do not need danger to rise more than proportionally. Across rows 3 to 5, assuming each reading’s pre-defence danger exceeds the leftover, that reading favours speed if and only if the capability share of the wait clears its threshold, with the inequality reversing for a reading if its leftover exceeds its pre-defence danger instead.

Opposite answers on misuse are not opposite verdicts on speed

Misuse is one entry in a larger ledger. Assume that a small change in speed has the same effect on the rest of the ledger under both readings, using the same cyber and facility specifications in each comparison. Also assume that the loss per misuse event is fixed. Then the two readings rank speed oppositely if and only if the net effect of speed on the rest of the ledger lies strictly between the two valued misuse effects (Figure 18). This holds however exposure is counted, and whether or not the misuse signs are opposite.

In my judgment, counted from arrival and under the equal-danger convention, the row 5 disagreement comes down to not knowing how strongly danger responds to speed. Without that convention, the relative scale of the two readings’ danger also enters. Counted from the start, these disagreements may, in my judgment, be a firmer core result than the unfinished construction described in Part 12.

How are these results checked?

The technical paper’s appendix records how each claim is supported: proved by hand, checked by a proof-checking program, computed, or an accounting rule. A proof-checking program confirms that a conclusion follows from the stated assumptions; it does not confirm that the assumptions hold in the world. Several headline results are proved by hand rather than by the program: the strict form of the plateau result under the level reading, the plateau result under the speed reading counted from the start, the defence race under the level reading and under the speed reading counted from the start, Result B, and the disagreements counted from the start.

Part 11. The evidence on misuse stops at task performance

Between a capable model and a health loss lie five separate claims:

  1. someone has access to the model;
  2. someone intends harm;
  3. the model helps with the relevant tasks;
  4. misuse actually happens;
  5. it costs health, in cases, deaths or healthy years.

The evidence reaches the third link and stops (Figure 19). I grade each piece of evidence STRONG, MODERATE or WEAK.

A strong benchmark, about an examination

On a virology benchmark, a publicly available model outperformed 94 per cent of expert virologists within their own sub-fields. That is STRONG as a benchmark result, but it gives no probability of an attack. The benchmark and the 2024 RAND trial also tested model generations that do not overlap. And the thresholds developers set for their own models are governance decisions, not measurements of risk.

Eight controlled trials, none measuring attack risk

Across the October 2026 search and a targeted search on 26 November 2026, seven works report eight controlled trials. Each compares people given access to a model with no-model or internet-only controls (or an unprinted comparator in one trial). Three trials state that people were randomly assigned, one randomises part of its sample, and four do not say how people were assigned.

  • The independent planning trial. Among the six trials of written planning or information access, only RAND’s 12-cell trial is independent of the developers whose models were tested. It found no significant difference in how workable the plans were. The estimated difference was minus 0.22 points on a 9-point scale. The design could detect a difference of about 1.0 point, roughly five times as large as the observed difference. Its authors write that their results “do not and could not disprove the existence of risk” (Mouton and others 2024). Graded MODERATE.
  • The physical-laboratory trial. In an 8-week randomised trial of 153 novices, 4 of 77 (5.2 per cent) with model access and 5 of 76 (6.6 per cent) without completed its core sequence of tasks. Its authors call it underpowered, and its interval is wide. Graded MODERATE.
  • Developer trials and a computer-only preprint. Four developer trials and a partly randomised computer-only preprint report higher scores than controls on some tasks. A fifth developer trial prints no control values. The four Anthropic trials report no plan free of critical failures, no plan judged likely to succeed, or model-assisted protocols that were not viable. Graded WEAK.

What do the individual trials report?

  • OpenAI’s test of GPT-4, with tasks built and scored by Gryphon Scientific, reports average gains of 0.88 (experts) and 0.25 (students) out of 10 in accuracy. None is statistically significant after correcting for multiple tests. The report gives neither the numerical test results, including the p-values used to judge statistical significance, nor ranges showing the uncertainty around these estimates.
  • Anthropic’s tests of its own models, run for its release decisions (with Anthropic staff among the participants in one trial and Deloitte designing or grading three), report point estimates of 42 per cent (plus or minus 11 per cent) and from 1.70 times to 2.53 times controls where controls are printed. They print no test statistic, p-value or defined interval (leaving “plus or minus” undefined in two trials).
  • Combining tasks, the computer-only preprint reports that the odds of a correct answer were 4.16 times as high with model help, with a 95 per cent uncertainty range from 2.63 to 6.87 times. Odds compare the chance of a correct answer with the chance of an incorrect one. But six of its eight benchmarks rest on 10 novices assigned by alternating, not at random. Of the two benchmarks with random assignment (47 people), one found no statistically significant effect, and for the other the report gives only a sub-task average that was not tested for significance. Novices with model help often scored below the models working alone. Its authors are at Scale AI, SecureBio (which also co-authored the virology benchmark), Oxford and UC Berkeley, and the excerpt read had no funding or competing-interest statement.
  • In the physical-laboratory trial, the completion rate with model access was 0.79 times the rate without it, with a 95 per cent uncertainty range of 0.24 to 2.62 times. Calculated after the trial, its chance of detecting a doubling of the odds of completion was about 36 per cent. It was funded by the Frontier Model Forum, Sentinel Bio and the Packard Foundation. Two funders sat on an advisory board that consulted on the design and authorised publication without holding authority over the design or how it was carried out, developer staff are thanked for design and operations help, and the authors declare no competing interests.

My reading of the record, not a derived result, is that the evidence so far suggests models help more with knowing and planning than with doing. None of the eight trials measures attack probability, casualties, or harm per unit of capability. So the misuse entries of the ledger remain unmeasured.

A reconstructed interval, and why a wide null is not a zero

The RAND trial prints a test statistic and a p-value but no interval. I reconstructed an approximate 95 per cent range from minus 1.5 to plus 1.0 points on its 9-point scale (Figure 20). That range rests on five assumptions and is graded WEAK as an interval.

The smallest effect a study can detect is a property of its design, under an assumed level of statistical power. It does not show that smaller effects are absent. The trials with no statistically significant main effect leave a wide range of effects on the measured tasks possible. They do not narrow the estimates of real-world misuse danger or harm per event. RAND’s result is compatible with a difference from roughly minus 1.5 to plus 1.0 points. The larger randomised trials, with 100 participants and 153 novices, print no interval or a wide one. Zero uplift (no extra help from a model over working without it) is compatible with these comparisons but not established by them. Reading an insensitive null as evidence of safety is an error, and the RAND authors do not make it.

No usable estimate of harm

The consensus report I read says the field lacks a standard. Uplift benchmarks are not standardised, and real-world impact is unclear because of secrecy, bans on testing, and immature evaluation methods. That gap depends on those conditions and could close. For now it means the misuse entries can be written down but not filled in.

One record of attempted misuse was found. In September 2026 the company reported disrupting several potential plots by scientists whose model-assisted research could have aided biological weapons, though it could not tell legitimate from malicious purposes. It is graded WEAK for three reasons:

  • I read a syndicated press account, with one paragraph unread, not the original report;
  • the count is only what an interested source detected and chose to report, with no denominator and no outcomes;
  • it bears on attempts, the fourth link, not on health loss.

It calibrates none of the misuse quantities. And nothing read settles whether the level reading or the speed reading is right. Both are carried as equals, and no mechanism behind the speed reading is modelled.

Part 12. Hospital ransomware raises in-hospital deaths, but its cost in healthy years can only be bracketed

One study shows cause and effect, and it exists in two versions

One study identifies the causal effect of ransomware attacks on hospital patients. Its working paper, which I read in full, covers 74 attacks on 163 US hospitals over 2016–2021, using Medicare fee-for-service claims, and was funded by the NIHCM Foundation. The study lines up hospitals by the dates they were attacked and uses individual admissions to compare changes with those at comparison hospitals. Its statistical uncertainty accounts for patients affected by the same attack. The attacks were found through news and federal reports, so undisclosed incidents are missing. The published article was read only in abstract, because its full text could not be obtained.

The two versions differ in method and in the size of the effect, so I never mix their figures:

  • the published abstract reports hospital volume down 17–24 per cent in the week of an attack, and the in-hospital death rate among patients already admitted up 34–38 per cent;
  • the working paper reports the in-hospital death rate up 0.77 percentage points from a 3.72 per cent baseline (p-value 0.07, with an interval that includes zero), or up 1.23 points from a 3.38 per cent baseline when later-attacked hospitals serve as controls (an interval that excludes zero).

On the full text read, the record is STRONG on the direction of the effect and MODERATE on its size.

About 0.6 to 0.9 extra deaths per attack, as a lower bound

The authors’ 2023 account puts the extra deaths at 42–67 Medicare patients over 2016–2021. A systematic review reports 69–76, taken from the unread published text. Dividing 42–67 by the 74 attacks gives 0.568 to 0.905 extra in-hospital Medicare deaths per attack. That is my arithmetic, graded WEAK. I did not divide the review’s count, because I could not check how many attacks the published version used. Either figure is a lower bound for all patients: it leaves out patients covered by other insurers, illness short of death, deaths after discharge, and patients sent elsewhere.

The working paper finds no significant effect on deaths within 30 days or on readmissions, and none among patients already in neighbouring hospitals. On my reading, the rise in in-hospital mortality together with no statistically significant rise in 30-day mortality is consistent with deaths being brought forward. That is my interpretation of the results. Studies of single incidents, with shorter outages and cruder measures, detect no difference in death rates. That fits an average across 74 attacks once the loss per attack is seen as varying from one attack to the next.

Patients move, trials slip, and the record has gaps

In California data covering all insurers, emergency visits fell 16.21 per cent at attacked hospitals in week 2 and rose by up to 7.10 per cent at nearby hospitals in week 3, recovering within eight weeks. The shift in patient numbers is STRONG evidence. What happened to the patients who moved rests on one event with tiny counts and is WEAK. One national attack cut clinical-trial referrals by 85 per cent and recruitment by 55 per cent, a finding based on ten survey responses and read only in abstract. In the ledger, that delays a therapy’s arrival rather than lowering its yearly benefit flow. Hospital quality measures worsened after data breaches. The authors propose the clean-up work as a possible cause, without observing it. Any such harm is booked once.

Ransomware attacks on US healthcare delivery organisations rose from 43 to 91 a year over 2016–2021, and 44.4 per cent of them disrupted care. No later count of disruptive attacks was found. No primary report of an AI-enabled cyberattack on a named hospital was found. The search found no source that converts hospital-attack deaths or illness into healthy years or reports how much healthy life the people who died had left.

The bracket on the death toll in healthy years

With no conversion found in the search, the calculation uses alternative estimates of how many healthy years each extra death costs. That turns on two choices:

  • what would otherwise have happened: did the attack bring a death forward by a short interval, change only where a patient died, or cause a death that would not otherwise have happened within the window?
  • how to value it: WHO’s standard years lost at the age of death, or the patients’ actual remaining life expectancy?

Under WHO’s life table, a death brought forward by some interval costs less than that interval. A death caused outright costs the full standard loss, 21.62 years for ages 70 to 74 (WHO 2024). The inpatients’ average age, 74.21, sits at the top of that band, so the high figures are somewhat overstated.

Estimate Extra deaths per attack Deaths brought forward by at most 30 days (a ceiling) Deaths caused outright
Main 0.568 0.047 12.3
More adverse 0.905 0.074 19.6

The last two columns are healthy years per attack, graded WEAK. Each figure is multiplied by an unmeasured factor, at least 1, that scales Medicare fee-for-service patients up to all patients. With an assumed actual life expectancy of 12 years, the high figures become 6.8 and 10.9. Under 95 per cent limits, the full spans run from 0 to 25.4 (main) and from 0.019 to 34.2 (more adverse).

Within each estimate, the two figures differ by a factor of about 260. That spread comes only from whether deaths were brought forward or caused. A shorter advance, or a change only in where patients die, pushes the loss toward zero, so the thirty-day figures are ceilings, not floors (Figure 21). The 30-day result can tell these cases apart only as far as that test had power, so neither reading is established or ruled out.

Why would a death brought forward cost so little?

If an attack hastens a death that would have come soon anyway, WHO’s life table counts the difference between the standard years lost at the two ages. That comes to less than the time by which the death was brought forward. Air-pollution epidemiology calls this mortality displacement, or “harvesting” (Zeger et al. 1999; Schwartz 2000). I cite those works only to show the idea exists. I checked their permanent publication identifiers without reading the articles. The factor of about 260 is 21.62 years divided by 30 days.

When misuse or hospitals would decide a comparison

Compare two options under the same modelling choices, and suppose misuse and hospital attacks pull in opposite directions while everything else stays fixed. Misuse decides the comparison, whatever the conversion between thirty days and the caused-outright figure, when its change in valued loss exceeds the change in hospital attacks valued at the top of the bracket. The hospital channel decides it when the misuse change falls below the hospital change valued at the thirty-day figure. Because a 30-day advance costs slightly less than 30 days under WHO’s table, that second case holds only if the standard loss per extra death is at least 30 days — which for displaced deaths requires an advance of more than 30 days (excluding a 30-day advance itself) — and it disappears under the main estimate’s 95 per cent range. If other entries also change and the two options stay on the same model branch, the first option has the lower balance when its extra misuse loss exceeds its net gain from the other entries after accounting for the change in hospital mortality losses.

A reversal of the whole balance is not established

The bracket is one of six parts of a larger construction. That construction asks whether plausible values of the unmeasured quantities could flip the sign of the balance between two speeds. The other five parts remain open:

  • fixing a target pair of speeds;
  • setting out the evidence formally;
  • writing worked cases that show a flip;
  • defining the smallest set of restrictions that would pin the sign down;
  • adding learning.

Part 13. Defence and benefit evidence leave the deciding quantities unmeasured

Defence: one well-dated programme, and no measured distances

In one vaccine programme, 66 days passed from the release of the viral sequence to the first clinical trial, and 326 days to rollout. A funder’s target is 100 days from recognising a threat to first authorisation. The fast early phase rested on years of earlier work on the vaccine platform. Those dates are STRONG for one disease, one platform and one programme. They show how long each milestone took, not which part of the clock was binding. So the model carries timings that are sequential, mixed and parallel. As noted in Running Through the Rain, fully sequential timing never reaches a point where adoption alone sets the wait.

One modelling study estimates 19.8 million deaths averted in the first year of COVID-19 vaccination (95 per cent interval 19.1 to 20.4 million), 79 per cent of them through direct protection, or over 14 million measured against reported deaths. That is in deaths, not healthy years. It bears on how coverage builds up and on gains against natural outbreaks, which are credited once.

The vaccine dates run from when the virus was recognised, not from the start of the model’s clock, so they do not bear on the defence race as modelled. No general pattern for how long recognition takes was found. That danger steps to a constant leftover level when a countermeasure lands is a modelling assumption, not a finding. One framework argues that the cyber pattern of patching may not carry over to biology, because some biological threats still lack any countermeasure. One mathematical model gives a condition for controlling an epidemic by isolation alone, under idealised assumptions. It covers one intervention in one model and sets no general limit on defence.

No measure of the defence distance was found. Nor was any dated record that sets a countermeasure’s capability requirement against the matching misuse requirement. Every version of the defence race needs the defence distance, and the speed-reading versions also need danger’s response to speed. My judgment is that the race cannot be tested on the evidence found, under either reading.

Benefit: most of the wait is clinical, and the health gained is unestimated

Clinical durations (STRONG). An analysis of 406,038 trial entries from 2000–2015 reports median durations of 1.6, 2.9 and 3.8 years for Phases 1, 2 and 3. Median total clinical time runs 5.9–7.2 years outside cancer and 13.1 years in cancer, and the overall chance of clinical success is 13.8 per cent. A separate accounting from before AI puts the clinical phase at roughly 95 months against 31 months for everything else. So most of the wait is clinical, which fits the earlier premise that capability is a minority of the time to patients. These pre-AI records do not measure what share of adoption time, including trials, approval and uptake, must run after capability arrives, though. The often-cited 17-year lag from research to practice comes with its reviewer’s caution that lag studies measure different end points (MODERATE).

Discovery speed-ups (WEAK). One programme, as reported by its developer, took roughly 18 months from finding a target to a preclinical candidate, and under 30 months to the end of its earliest human trials (phase 0/1). A review’s claim of 30–70 per cent cuts in early timelines traces back to no primary study that can be checked. No estimate across drugs of AI’s effect on total development time was found. Later clinical trials are reported to take about as long as in conventional development. And a prominent outside study of AI-accelerated materials discovery was withdrawn by its institution. Nothing here shows AI shortening the whole path from target to approval.

Chance of success (MODERATE). In abstract-level sources, candidates discovered with AI show Phase I success rates of 80–90 per cent. That is above historical averages, and fits a filter for safety rather than a gain in effectiveness. Their Phase II success is about 40 per cent on a small sample, similar to historical averages. An author on the developer side states that none had been approved as of December 2024. Three sources from different directions suggest that choosing the right compound matters more than speed. That is why the model fixes the success probability rather than letting it vary with speed.

Health gained (unestimated). No estimate of healthy years gained from AI across a population was found. Across 48 economic evaluations of narrow clinical tools, an abstract-level review that flags systematic optimism reports that the middle half of results ran from 0.001 to 0.019 quality-adjusted life years gained, with years weighted by the quality of life during them. A second review finds that most such studies rest on models rather than observed patient outcomes. The clinical results realised so far come mostly from narrow, single-task tools. Evidence for general-purpose models is at the level of written case scenarios or laboratory tests. In one randomised trial, 50 physicians given a 2023 large language model as a diagnostic aid did not score significantly better than controls (adjusted difference 2 points, 95 per cent interval from minus 4 to plus 8).

Part 14. Laboratories and policy levers can be read only conditionally

The developer’s laboratory

No source found ranks a developer’s laboratory against a public or academic one for safety. So the model evaluates the laboratory at a fixed speed, through the two distances of Part 8. Whether a laboratory instead changes the speed of the biology clocks locally is left open. The defence-distance effect has one form under all three choices, while the misuse-distance effect depends on each. For the reported laboratory, no independent record shows what it does or which distance it moves.

Under US law, a privately funded laboratory at biosafety level 1 or 2 that holds no listed agent falls outside the select-agent rules and outside the oversight that comes with federal funding. That leaves general workplace-safety guidance and guidance on research with DNA assembled by joining separate pieces. The source notes that this guidance has no enforceable penalties. Whether any particular facility triggers either rule depends on facts about its funding and holdings that are unverified. Canada licenses by activity. The rules for screening DNA synthesis orders, as of the 26 October 2026 search date, are unresolved in the texts held.

Even a known sign for the distance effect would leave the laboratory’s whole ledger open. That ledger also carries changes in benefit, including withholding, and facility losses from accidents and harm to workers. The comparison with a public equivalent stays open too.

Countermeasure programmes and oversight

The model has no shared budget across levers, and the quantities that would decide between them are unmeasured. So it does not rank these levers against each other or against speed.

A countermeasure programme (I5) acts on deployment time, on how much of adoption runs after capability arrives, and on the defence distance. Suppose the countermeasure lands after misuse arrives and inside the window, with a fixed leftover. Two effects of the defence distance then have to be kept apart:

  • At a fixed speed: a shorter defence distance lowers misuse loss while the countermeasure waits on capability and plateau danger exceeds the leftover (Part 8).
  • Under the level reading, for the speed question: a longer defence distance makes speeding up more favourable while the countermeasure waits on capability and plateau danger exceeds the leftover, because it leaves more of the deployment wait for speed to shorten (Part 7).

Under the speed reading counted from the start, when the countermeasure has its own defence distance and waits on capability, that distance works through Part 7’s ceiling on how strongly danger can respond to speed before speeding up raises loss. A longer distance raises that ceiling when some adoption runs after capability arrives and danger exceeds the leftover, and lowers speed’s effect on misuse loss if and only if danger’s response to speed is also below the share of danger the countermeasure removes.

Cuts to the defence distance stop helping once the countermeasure is waiting on adoption. I checked the simple rule that the cut to the defence distance must exceed the cut to the misuse distance, with danger counted from arrival and no danger left after deployment. In the speed reading and the two convention-A cases tested, the rule and the full calculation disagreed 46 times on whether loss rose or fell. All 46 occurred when a cut crossed into the adoption branch. Shortening deployment time lowers misuse loss and raises gains against natural outbreaks only if bringing deployment forward moves coverage in one direction, towards more coverage. The dates from a single vaccine programme do not establish that response.

Oversight and screening (I6) target facility event rates or the danger of misuse. Closing the US funding trigger would change which facilities oversight reaches. Screening DNA synthesis orders acts at the point where digital designs become physical material. The treaty imposes prevention duties on each country without checking individual facilities. Under the mapping the model assumes, I6 does not move the defence distance, and the size of its effect is unmeasured.

Part 15. What I do not claim, and what would change the answer

How far the search went

The search covered seven literatures. The first search, on 26 October 2026, found 173 source records across 162 distinct works. Of those records, 22 were read in full, 113 in part, 17 only in abstract, and 21 could not be obtained. A targeted search on 26 November 2026 added six works reporting seven controlled trials, read in excerpt. Works that could not be obtained are listed only as such, never used as evidence, and findings resting on abstracts or second-hand accounts are labelled throughout. “Unmeasured” always means that no measure was found in the documented search, a statement about the search rather than the world.

What was excluded, and what a safety classifier stopped

On safety grounds I excluded operational detail about biological and cyber attacks. One source was kept only as a safe excerpt. The 2024 RAND trial was read for its design, scoring rules and statistics, without opening its section on model outputs. For the works added in November, a model’s safety classifier stopped two of the reads, which were then completed on another model, and the readers were given excerpts without the laboratory-method sections. A safety classifier also interrupted some drafting and summarising steps. As a result, one methodological criticism was applied by reference rather than worked out again.

Ordinary gaps

  • The published version of the hospital study was read only in abstract.
  • The RAND trial prints no interval or standard error, and five developer trials print neither a test statistic nor a defined interval.
  • Incident updates from one national health service were blocked.
  • The US rules for screening DNA synthesis orders, as of the search date, could not be confirmed from primary documents, and neither could a laboratory-safety manual.
  • Two studies on the benefit side were behind paywalls.
  • The 2026 edition of the international AI safety report was not read.

What the model leaves out

  • How bad each misuse event is stays fixed. Severity that rises with capability is left out.
  • Learning is not modelled, and adding it is one of the open parts of the construction in Part 12.
  • Countermeasures that must wait for a particular agent to be identified fall outside the defence race and the facility comparison, which stay open for them.
  • There is no shared budget across levers, so no ranking of levers.
  • The cost of a public laboratory’s openness in spreading dual-use knowledge is not included, so the ledger supports no comparison of a developer’s laboratory with a public one.
  • No decision rule is adopted, and maximin is not worked out.

What would settle what

Figure 22 matches the main unmeasured quantities to the part of the argument each would decide. They are:

  • Benefit: the therapy’s yearly health flow, its chance of success, how long it waits on capability, its adoption time and the share of that adoption wait that runs after capability arrives, and the share withheld by a developer’s laboratory.
  • Hospitals: baseline care lost per attack, the benefit forgone during outages, trial delays, and the rate of hospital attacks. Also unmeasured is the share of patients’ time on a new therapy that outages interrupt.
  • Misuse: the danger and the misuse distance, the loss per misuse event, and how strongly danger responds to speed.
  • Defence: the defence schedule (time to recognition, coverage, leftover danger, deployment time and the share of it that runs after capability arrives) and the defence distance.
  • Facilities and outbreaks: facility accidents, harm to workers, and gains against natural outbreaks. For facilities, both how often releases and worker-harm events happen and how much health each event costs are unmeasured.
  • The specification itself: whether misuse risk follows the level reached or the speed of advance.

Some links are already clear from the earlier parts. The defence race needs the defence distance, and under the speed reading it also needs danger’s response to speed. Within each specification, the 260-fold spread in the hospital bracket comes from not knowing how many healthy years each extra death costs. Whether a reversal of the whole balance lies within the evidence also remains open.

The window’s length is a choice, not a gap in the search. Truncation exists only when the misuse threshold lies beyond what the window reaches at current speed, and the speed reading’s benefit-against-misuse test can flip as the window lengthens.

Part 16. What to take away

  • Once biological misuse, facility releases and hospital attacks are counted, the narrow case for speed made in Running Through the Rain may or may not survive: on what has been measured, that cannot be determined, and I adopt no rule for acting.
  • In the model, some results hold under every open choice, each with its stated conditions:
    • once misuse capability arrives inside the window and danger stays open, faster progress adds misuse loss under the level reading if plateau danger exceeds the climb’s average, and under the speed reading if danger rises with speed;
    • while a countermeasure waits on adoption, if it follows misuse arrival and lands before the window ends with fixed leftover danger, faster progress adds misuse loss when the plateau exceeds the climb’s average under the level reading, or when danger rises with speed under the speed reading;
    • at a fixed speed, with a deployment date independent of the misuse distance and between misuse arrival and the end of the window, the same rule applies across the choices. Shortening the defence distance lowers misuse loss while the countermeasure waits on capability and reduces danger to a fixed lower level;
    • for an ongoing benefit from a therapy still waiting on capability and arriving inside the window if there is one, discounting raises the weight on earlier arrival relative to the chance of success;
    • undiscounted, a fixed-length benefit counted in full gains nothing from arriving earlier;
    • each health change is counted once.
    The defence results cover only countermeasures that need not wait for a particular agent to be identified.
  • The earlier ranking can reverse in four ways: through time spent on the plateau, through truncation (level reading, counted from the start, with a finite window), through a countermeasure that is stuck in adoption or does not respond enough to speed, or through hospital and facility harms. The speed result and the facility result do not settle each other in one direction under the speed reading and in both directions under the level reading with convention A counted from the start.
  • With danger counted from arrival and the level reading gated, only row 5 can give strictly opposite effects of speed on misuse. Wider disagreement rests on counting full-strength speed-reading danger from the start, before misuse capability arrives, a premise unsettled for biology. In the plateau and truncation cases, that disagreement also requires danger to fall somewhere along the capability climb. With fixed loss per event and a common effect of speed on the other entries, the readings rank speed oppositely if and only if that common effect lies strictly between the two valued effects of speed on misuse.
  • An undiscounted comparison tilts toward harms when it counts all life-years lost to deaths inside the window but only the benefit gained before the window ends.
  • The death toll of hospital attacks is only bracketed, and misuse is unmeasured.

Where to read more

  • Running Toward the Clinic: Speed, Biological Risk and Health in the AI Transition, the technical paper behind this guide, with the formal set-up, proofs, numerical checks and full tables in its appendices.
  • Running Through the Rain: Speed, Secrecy and Risk in the AI Cyber Transition, from which I take the cyber loss count and its speed threshold, the health balance, the split of each wait into capability and adoption parts, the counting window, and the level reading of danger as an alternative.
